propositions.text: Whether toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. exempting appellant from criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: the Court must decide whether a toxic psychosis that results from a state of self‑induced intoxication caused by an accused person’s use of chemical drugs constitutes a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 of the Criminal Code

propositions.text: Review the scopes of insanity defence and self-induced intoxication defence generally.
propositions.quote: this case also gives the Court an opportunity to review the respective scopes of the insanity defence and the defence of self‑induced intoxication

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication qualifies as a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. and review insanity and intoxication defences.

propositions.text: Appellant assaulted two individuals in psychotic condition caused by drugs taken hours earlier, seriously injuring one.
propositions.quote: The appellant brutally assaulted two individuals while he was in a psychotic condition caused by chemical drugs he had taken a few hours earlier

propositions.text: Appellant was convicted on two counts of aggravated assault and assault by Court of Québec.
propositions.quote: After being convicted by the Court of Québec on two counts of aggravated assault and assault

propositions.text: Appellant unsuccessfully appealed to Quebec Court of Appeal for verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder.
propositions.quote: the appellant tried unsuccessfully on appeal to obtain a verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder

propositions.text: Appellant appeals to Supreme Court against Quebec Court of Appeal judgment rejecting toxic psychosis as 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the appellant is now appealing the judgment of the Quebec Court of Appeal, which rejected the argument that a toxic psychosis resulting from the voluntary consumption of drugs is a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant assaulted two people in drug-induced psychosis, was convicted, unsuccessfully appealed, and now appeals to Supreme Court on 'mental disorder' issue.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal's judgment is correct in law and the appeal should be dismissed.
propositions.quote: I find that the judgment of the Court of Appeal is correct in law. I would therefore dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Court of Appeal's judgment correct and would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant and acquaintance smoked marijuana and took amphetamines on October 23, 2005, then traveled while intoxicated.
propositions.quote: the appellant, Tommy Bouchard‑Lebrun, and a long‑time acquaintance of his, Yohann Schmouth, had smoked marijuana and taken amphetamines during the day on October 23, 2005

propositions.text: They took bus from Rivière-du-Loup to Mont-Joli while still intoxicated.
propositions.quote: They took the bus from Rivière‑du‑Loup, where the appellant lived, to the last stop in Mont‑Joli. They were still intoxicated when they got on the bus.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant and acquaintance used drugs on October 23 and traveled intoxicated by bus to Mont-Joli.

propositions.text: At 1:30 a.m., Gilles Tremblay picked up appellant and friend; no signs of intoxication apparent then.
propositions.quote: At about 1:30 a.m., Gilles Tremblay, an old acquaintance of the appellant’s family, picked them up in his car. At that time, no signs of intoxication were apparent from the appellant’s behaviour.

propositions.text: Witnesses confirmed appellant was 'OK' around Val-Brillant; drug effects from October 23 had ceased before arrival in Amqui.
propositions.quote: His statements confirmed Mr. Schmouth’s testimony that the appellant was [translation] “OK” again when they were around Val‑Brillant

paragraphs.summary: At 1:30 a.m., appellant showed no intoxication signs; witnesses confirmed drug effects had ceased before Amqui arrival.

propositions.text: In Amqui, appellant and friend bought and took ecstasy pills called 'poire bleue' on October 24 night.
propositions.quote: In Amqui, the two young men purchased ecstasy pills of a type known as “poire bleue”, which they took during the night on October 24.

propositions.text: They decided to attack Dany Lévesque for real or imagined reason of wearing an 'upside-down cross'.
propositions.quote: the appellant and Mr. Schmouth decided to go and beat up Dany Lévesque, who was known as “Pee‑Wee”, for the real or imagined reason that he wore an [translation] “upside‑down cross” around his neck.

propositions.text: At 5:00 a.m., they illegally entered Lévesque's building and attacked him.
propositions.quote: Around 5:00 a.m., the appellant and Mr. Schmouth illegally entered the building where Mr. Lévesque lived

paragraphs.summary: In Amqui, appellant took ecstasy, then attacked Lévesque for wearing an 'upside-down cross' after illegally entering his building.

propositions.text: Mr. Dumas tried to intervene; appellant threw him down stairs and stomped on his head, causing permanent disability.
propositions.quote: The appellant grabbed him and threw him violently down the stairs. Mr. Dumas lay on the floor at the bottom of the stairs. The appellant went down to where he was and stomped on his head.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant violently threw Mr. Dumas down stairs and stomped his head, causing permanent disability.

propositions.text: At assault time, appellant was highly intoxicated from 'poire bleue' pill causing dissociation from reality.
propositions.quote: At the time of the assault, the appellant was highly intoxicated because of the effects of the “poire bleue” pill he had taken a few hours earlier.

propositions.text: Appellant described being 'on another planet' with dissociation between perceptions and reality after pill.
propositions.quote: he was [translation] “on another planet”

propositions.text: Two trial witnesses said appellant 'started acting weird' and was 'completely out of it' after taking pill.
propositions.quote: Two witnesses at the trial stated that he [translation] “started acting weird” and was “completely out of it” after taking the “poire bleue” pill.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant was highly intoxicated and dissociated from reality after taking 'poire bleue'; witnesses confirmed odd behavior.

propositions.text: Appellant had religious delirium symptoms, obsessed with 'upside-down cross' and made absurd religious statements during attack.
propositions.quote: the appellant experienced an episode that might be described as religious delirium in light of its symptoms

propositions.text: He made absurd but coherent religious statements, blessed victim's spouse, and left calmly after attack.
propositions.quote: he blessed Mr. Dumas’s spouse by making the sign of the cross on her forehead... he then left the scene very calmly as if nothing had just happened.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant had religious delirium with absurd statements, blessed victim's spouse, and left calmly after attack.

propositions.text: No dispute appellant was in serious psychotic condition at offence time, effects diminished by October 28, 2005.
propositions.quote: It has never been in dispute, in any of the courts, that the appellant was in a serious psychotic condition at the time of the offences and that the effects of that condition diminished gradually until they disappeared on October 28, 2005.

propositions.text: Essential issue is how psychosis affects appellant's criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: The essential issue in this appeal is instead how that psychosis affects the appellant’s criminal responsibility.

propositions.text: Appellant had no prior psychotic episodes, no underlying mental disease, no addiction, and was an occasional drug user.
propositions.quote: the appellant had never experienced a psychotic episode such as this prior to the incidents in question. He had no underlying disease of the mind, nor was he addicted to a particular substance.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant was in serious psychosis at offence time with no prior episodes or addiction; issue is effect on responsibility.

propositions.text: Appellant charged with aggravated assault, assault, breaking and entering with intent, and attempted breaking and entering.
propositions.quote: the appellant was charged with committing aggravated assault on Mr. Dumas and Mr. Lévesque... and with breaking and entering a dwelling‑house with intent to commit an indictable offence and attempting to break and enter a place other than a dwelling-house

propositions.text: Appellant pleaded not guilty to all charges.
propositions.quote: He pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant charged with multiple offences and pleaded not guilty to all.

propositions.text: At trial, appellant admitted acts but claimed psychotic condition from friend's spiritual influence prevented judgment.
propositions.quote: he claimed that, at the time, he had been under the effects of a psychotic condition induced by Mr. Schmouth’s spiritual influence

propositions.text: Defence argued psychotic condition prevented appellant from assessing drug-taking impact, exempting him from liability.
propositions.quote: this psychotic condition had prevented the appellant from exercising judgment to assess what impact his drug‑taking on October 23 and 24, 2005 might have

paragraphs.summary: At trial, appellant admitted acts but claimed psychosis from friend's spiritual influence exempted him from liability.

propositions.text: Two psychiatrists agreed appellant was severely psychotic and incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at offence time.
propositions.quote: They were in agreement that the appellant had been suffering from [translation] “a severe psychosis that made him incapable of distinguishing right from wrong”

propositions.text: Defence expert said psychosis mainly from mystical atmosphere and friend's control influenced drug-taking decision.
propositions.quote: Dr. Roger Turmel, the defence’s expert, stated that the appellant’s psychosis had resulted mainly from [translation] “the mystical atmosphere” into which he had been plunged by Mr. Schmouth

propositions.text: Crown expert disagreed, said no third party influence; psychosis was toxic from substance consumption.
propositions.quote: According to Dr. Sylvain Faucher, the circumstances required for psychosis resulting from a third party’s influence were not present in this case. He concluded instead that... the appellant had been suffering from toxic psychosis

paragraphs.summary: Psychiatrists agreed appellant was psychotic and incapable of right/wrong; defence said mystical influence, Crown said toxic psychosis.

propositions.text: Judge Decoste accepted Crown expert's opinion that appellant had toxic psychosis at offence time.
propositions.quote: Judge Decoste accepted Dr. Faucher’s opinion and found that the appellant had been suffering from toxic psychosis at the time he committed the offences

propositions.text: Appellant acquitted on breaking and entering counts due to extreme intoxication.
propositions.quote: because of that state of extreme intoxication, the appellant had to be acquitted on the counts of breaking and entering with intent to commit a criminal offence and attempting to break and enter

propositions.text: Appellant convicted on aggravated assault and assault counts, relying on s.33.1 Cr. C. that self-induced intoxication is no defence for bodily harm offences.
propositions.quote: He then convicted the appellant on the counts of aggravated assault on Mr. Dumas and assault on Mr. Lévesque, referring for that purpose to s. 33.1 Cr. C., which provides that self‑induced intoxication cannot be a defence to an offence against the bodily integrity of another person

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found toxic psychosis, acquitted appellant on breaking and entering, convicted on assaults citing s.33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Judge Decoste sentenced appellant to five years for aggravated assault and three months concurrent for common assault.
propositions.quote: Judge Decoste sentenced the appellant to imprisonment for five years for the offence of aggravated assault and three months concurrent for that of common assault.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge sentenced appellant to five years for aggravated assault and three months concurrent for assault.

propositions.text: Appellant appealed guilty verdict and sentence to Quebec Court of Appeal, changing defence argument.
propositions.quote: The appellant appealed the guilty verdict and the related sentence to the Quebec Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant conceded toxic psychosis but argued mental disorder defence should apply as he was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong.
propositions.quote: he no longer claimed that his psychotic condition had resulted from Mr. Schmouth’s spiritual influence... he instead argued that the defence of mental disorder should have been applicable

paragraphs.summary: Appellant appealed, conceding toxic psychosis but arguing mental disorder defence applied due to incapacity to distinguish right/wrong.

propositions.text: Appellant argued trial judge confused insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C. with self-induced intoxication defence under s.33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the appellant argued that the trial judge had confused the insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. with the defence of self‑induced intoxication under s. 33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Appellant asked Court of Appeal to disregard s.33.1 and find toxic psychosis a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: He therefore asked the Court of Appeal to disregard s. 33.1 and find that he was not criminally responsible on the basis that his toxic psychosis... was a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argued trial judge confused defences and asked Court of Appeal to find toxic psychosis a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal disagreed that psychotic condition was unforeseeable; expert evidence showed high risk of psychosis from drug use.
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A., writing for the court, began by expressing disagreement with the premise... that the development of a psychotic condition was “unforeseeable”

propositions.text: Expert testified 50% of PCP users and 13% of amphetamine users likely develop psychosis; appellant seemed one of them.
propositions.quote: Dr. Faucher’s testimony had proved that 50 percent of PCP users and 13 percent of amphetamine users were likely to develop such a condition

propositions.text: Appellant's psychosis effects lasted as long as intoxication lasted.
propositions.quote: the effects of his psychosis had lasted as long as he had remained intoxicated

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found psychosis was foreseeable and appellant was among those likely to develop it, lasting as long as intoxication.

propositions.text: Defence of self-induced intoxication available in extreme cases for general intent offences per R. v. Daviault.
propositions.quote: according to the line of authority based on R. v. Daviault... the defence of self‑induced intoxication was available in extreme cases to accused persons charged with general intent offences

propositions.text: Parliament limited self-induced intoxication defence to non-violent offences by enacting s.33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the enactment by Parliament of s. 33.1 Cr. C. had limited this defence to non‑violent offences

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal noted self-induced intoxication defence is limited to non-violent offences by s.33.1 Cr. C., per R. v. Daviault.

propositions.text: Insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C. applies to underlying mental disorder worsened by drug use.
propositions.quote: the courts had held that the defence was available to an accused person suffering from an underlying mental disorder whose mental condition had “deteriorated even more” as a result of drug use

propositions.text: Cooper v. The Queen held transitory drug-induced psychosis is not a 'disease of the mind' under ss.2 and 16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: this Court had clearly held in Cooper v. The Queen... that transitory psychosis induced by drug use cannot be considered a “disease of the mind” within the meaning of ss. 2 and 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held appellant's toxic psychosis did not qualify for insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: she accordingly held that because of the appellant’s psychotic condition at the time he assaulted his victims, his insanity defence under s. 16 of the Criminal Code could not succeed.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal held transitory drug-induced psychosis is not a 'disease of the mind' and appellant's insanity defence failed.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. found appellant had no underlying disease of the mind and became sane after intoxication effects passed
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A. added that the appellant had no underlying disease of the mind and had become perfectly sane again once the effects of the “poire bleue” had passed.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. found appellant's argument was an attempt to circumvent Parliament's intent to preclude self-induced intoxication defence
propositions.quote: the appellant’s argument was an attempt to circumvent Parliament’s intent by making it possible for an accused person to plead self‑induced intoxication to avoid criminal liability

paragraphs.summary: Thibault J.A. found appellant had no underlying mental disease and that appellant's argument tried to circumvent Parliament's intent to preclude self-induced intoxication defence.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal dismissed appeal against sentence as sentences were harsh but not unreasonable
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal also dismissed the appeal against sentence on the basis that the sentences imposed by the trial judge, though harsh, were not unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal dismissed appeal against sentence as sentences were harsh but not unreasonable.

propositions.text: Does s. 33.1 Cr. C. limit defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder under s. 16 Cr. C.?
propositions.quote: Does s. 33.1 Cr. C. limit the scope of the defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder provided for in s. 16 Cr. C.?

propositions.text: Can toxic psychosis caused by self-induced intoxication be a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.?
propositions.quote: Can a toxic psychosis whose symptoms are caused by a state of self‑induced intoxication be a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.?

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies two issues: whether s. 33.1 limits mental disorder defence under s. 16, and whether toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication is a mental disorder under s. 16.

propositions.text: Appellant concedes toxic psychosis resulted exclusively from self-induced intoxication on October 24, 2005
propositions.quote: The appellant concedes that the evidence in the record shows that his toxic psychosis resulted exclusively from his state of self‑induced intoxication the night of October 24, 2005.

propositions.text: Appellant disagrees courts failed to consider predisposition but does not argue intoxication triggered latent disease of mind
propositions.quote: he is not specifically submitting that they erred in rejecting the argument that his intoxication had triggered a latent disease of the mind

propositions.text: Appellant's counsel stated no ground of appeal on latent disease of mind at hearing
propositions.quote: his counsel stated at the hearing in this Court that she was not raising this as a ground of appeal

paragraphs.summary: Appellant concedes toxic psychosis was from self-induced intoxication and does not appeal on latent disease of mind argument.

propositions.text: Appellant argues single intoxication episode causing toxic psychosis can be a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: a single episode of intoxication can be a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. if it produces abnormal effects on the accused, such as psychotic symptoms

propositions.text: Appellant's syllogism: toxic psychosis affects only vulnerable psyches, so it must be a legal mental disorder
propositions.quote: since toxic psychosis is an abnormal effect of intoxication, it necessarily affects only those whose psyches are particularly fragile or vulnerable

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues toxic psychosis from intoxication is a mental disorder legally because it affects only vulnerable individuals.

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis results from underlying disease of mind revealed by intoxication
propositions.quote: the toxic psychosis he developed after taking a “poire bleue” pill resulted from an underlying disease of the mind that became apparent as a result of his intoxication

propositions.text: Appellant relies on general argument that any toxic psychosis from single intoxication episode is a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: any toxic psychosis, even one that results, as the trial judge found in this case, from a single episode of intoxication, must be considered a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Appellant's premise: intoxication never causes toxic psychosis; it must originate in pre-existing mental condition
propositions.quote: intoxication can never be the real or underlying cause of toxic psychosis and that toxic psychosis must originate in a pre‑existing mental condition

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues toxic psychosis results from underlying mental disease, not intoxication, and any toxic psychosis is a mental disorder under s. 16.

propositions.text: Appellant contends psychotic condition should never legally be considered mere intoxication
propositions.quote: a person in a psychotic condition should never, from a legal standpoint, be considered merely to be intoxicated

propositions.text: Appellant argues Court of Appeal confused self-induced intoxication defence with mental disorder defence under s. 16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal confused the defence of self‑induced intoxication with that of mental disorder under s. 16 Cr. C. in holding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. applied in this case

propositions.text: Appellant argues Thibault J.A. erred in saying s. 33.1 Cr. C. prevents intoxication defence and limits mental disorder defence
propositions.quote: [h]is submission would have the effect of rendering s. 33.1 Cr. C. meaningless and [disregarding] the clearly expressed legislative intent

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues psychosis should not be mere intoxication legally and Court of Appeal confused defences, misapplying s. 33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Appellant says s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses Daviault dissent that self-induced intoxication defence unavailable for general intent offences
propositions.quote: Parliament, in enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C., endorsed the position taken by the dissenting judges in Daviault

propositions.text: Appellant says dissent acknowledged toxic psychosis remains a defence under s. 16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: those dissenting judges had acknowledged that “toxic psychosis remained a defence under s. 16”

propositions.text: Appellant submits dissent balanced punishing voluntary intoxication but not punishing those lacking mental capacity
propositions.quote: the dissent in Daviault struck a judicious balance and gave effect to society’s wish to punish reprehensible acts committed by persons who decide voluntarily to become intoxicated, but not to punish those who lack the mental capacity

propositions.text: Appellant cites Sopinka J. dissent that intoxication-induced mental illness affects fragile, vulnerable individuals
propositions.quote: Sopinka J.’s reasons support his position that “those who become mentally ill as a result of drug use are fragile and vulnerable individuals who are predisposed to mental disorders”

propositions.text: Appellant raises no constitutional challenge to s. 33.1 Cr. C., only interpretation and application
propositions.quote: But the appellant raises no arguments regarding the constitutionality of s. 33.1 Cr. C., which means that only the interpretation and application of that provision are in issue.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses Daviault dissent that toxic psychosis remains a defence, balancing punishment and mental incapacity, raising no constitutional issues.

propositions.text: Summarizes case law leading to s. 33.1 Cr. C. enactment, starting with House of Lords decision in DPP v. Beard
propositions.quote: it will be helpful to briefly summarize the case law that led to the enactment of that provision. There are three seminal cases in this regard. The first is the decision of the House of Lords in Director of Public Prosecutions v. Beard

propositions.text: Lord Birkenhead's three rules from Beard: intoxication can ground insanity defence if it produces disease of mind; drunkenness affecting specific intent considered; drunkenness short of incapacity does not rebut intent presumption
propositions.quote: Lord Birkenhead set out the following three rules (as summarized by Bastarache J. in R. v. Daley): (1) intoxication could be a ground for an insanity defence if it produced a disease of the mind. (2) evidence of drunkenness which renders the accused incapable of forming the specific intent essential to constitute the crime should be taken into consideration. (3) drunkenness falling short of incapacity does not rebut presumption of intent.

paragraphs.summary: Court summarizes case law leading to s. 33.1 Cr. C., including Beard's three rules on intoxication and insanity defence.

propositions.text: Beard principle: intoxication can be defence for specific intent offence, subject to Robinson qualification
propositions.quote: intoxication can be raised as a defence in respect of a specific intent offence in certain circumstances

propositions.text: Robinson held Beard's third rule violated Charter ss. 7 and 11(d), replaced with rule intoxication can be defence if it prevented forming actual specific intent
propositions.quote: Robinson held that the third of the rules from Beard... violated ss. 7 and 11 (d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms... intoxication can be a defence if it prevented the accused from forming the actual specific intent

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Beard principle on intoxication defence and Robinson's Charter-based modification of that rule.

propositions.text: Since Beard, intoxication defence applies to specific intent offences; Leary held self-induced intoxication cannot raise doubt on mens rea for general intent offences
propositions.quote: it has thus been possible to apply the intoxication defence to acquit an accused charged with a specific intent offence... Leary answered this question in the negative

propositions.text: Leary established recklessness in becoming intoxicated can constitute fault for general intent offence
propositions.quote: the recklessness shown by an accused in becoming voluntarily intoxicated can constitute the fault element needed to find that a general intent offence has been committed

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Leary rule that self-induced intoxication cannot negate mens rea for general intent offences, recklessness suffices.

propositions.text: Daviault majority held Leary rule violated Charter ss. 7 and 11(d), allowing intoxication akin to automatism or insanity to raise reasonable doubt for general intent offences
propositions.quote: a majority of the Court held that the “substituted mens rea” rule from Leary was contrary to ss. 7 and 11 (d) of the Charter... accused persons who were in a “state akin to automatism or insanity”... would be legally entitled to raise a reasonable doubt

paragraphs.summary: Daviault majority held Leary rule unconstitutional, allowing intoxication akin to automatism or insanity to raise reasonable doubt for general intent offences.

propositions.text: Sopinka J. dissented in Daviault, supporting Leary rule and emphasizing society's right to punish voluntary intoxication
propositions.quote: Sopinka J. wrote a strong dissent in Daviault... application of that rule did not relieve the Crown of the responsibility... society’s right “to punish those who of their own free will render themselves so intoxicated”

paragraphs.summary: Sopinka J. dissented in Daviault, supporting Leary rule and emphasizing punishing voluntary intoxication.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to prevent intoxication defence for general intent violent crimes
propositions.quote: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to ensure that “intoxication may never be used as a defence against general intent violent crimes such as sexual assault and assault”

propositions.text: Section 33.1 Cr. C. prohibits defence of self-induced intoxication for offences involving interference with bodily integrity where accused departed markedly from reasonable care
propositions.quote: 33.1 (1) It is not a defence... that the accused, by reason of self‑induced intoxication, lacked the general intent... where the accused departed markedly from the standard of care... (2) person departs markedly from reasonable care where intoxicated and interferes with bodily integrity of another

paragraphs.summary: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to bar intoxication defence for violent general intent offences involving bodily integrity interference.

propositions.text: Appellant can argue Parliament implicitly endorsed Sopinka J.'s dissent by enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the appellant can reasonably argue that Parliament implicitly endorsed Sopinka J.’s dissent in Daviault by enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Enactment of s. 33.1 Cr. C. limited majority Daviault rule; did not revive Leary rule or codify dissent
propositions.quote: It did not actually codify the position taken by the dissenting judges in Daviault; rather, it limited the scope of the rule stated by the majority.

propositions.text: Daviault principles still state of law except for s. 33.1 Cr. C. restriction; example is appellant's acquittal on property charges
propositions.quote: Daviault would still apply today... The fact that the appellant was acquitted at trial on the charges... affords an eloquent example of this.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 33.1 Cr. C. limits Daviault majority rule but does not revive Leary; Daviault still applies except for s. 33.1 restriction.

propositions.text: s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not be interpreted to limit scope of s. 16 Cr. C.; intoxication and insanity are distinct defences with different principles
propositions.quote: s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not be interpreted so as to limit the scope of s. 16 Cr. C. Intoxication and insanity are two distinct legal concepts.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not limit s. 16 Cr. C.; intoxication and insanity are distinct defences.

propositions.text: Application of s. 16 Cr. C. and s. 33.1 Cr. C. are mutually exclusive; s. 33.1 applies if intoxication caused lack of general intent or voluntariness
propositions.quote: application of s. 16 Cr. C. and that of s. 33.1 Cr. C. are mutually exclusive... For s. 33.1 Cr. C. to apply, the court must conclude... lack of general intent or voluntariness by reason of self‑induced intoxication

propositions.text: Absence of intent or voluntariness precludes finding incapacity caused by disease of mind (R. v. Huppie)
propositions.quote: The absence of this intent or voluntariness would then preclude a finding that the incapacity of the accused was caused by a disease of the mind (R. v. Huppie)

propositions.text: Intoxication cannot support s. 33.1 application if accused proves incapacity from mental disorder
propositions.quote: the fact that an accused was intoxicated... cannot support a finding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. applies if the accused establishes that he or she was incapable... by reason of a mental disorder.

paragraphs.summary: Court states s. 16 and s. 33.1 Cr. C. defences are mutually exclusive; intoxication defence applies only if no mental disorder incapacity.

propositions.text: Court must identify source of psychosis—self-induced intoxication or disease of mind—to determine criminal responsibility
propositions.quote: the problem the court faces is to identify a specific source for his or her mental condition... self‑induced intoxication or a disease of the mind

propositions.text: Identification is difficult when mental health was precarious before intoxication and psychosis emerged during intoxication
propositions.quote: This appears to be all the more difficult to do in cases in which the mental health of the accused was already precarious... and in which the psychosis emerged while the accused was highly intoxicated.

propositions.text: Source identification determines whether accused held criminally responsible
propositions.quote: this identification of the source of the psychosis plays a key role, since it will ultimately determine whether the accused will be held criminally responsible for his or her actions.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains difficulty and importance of identifying psychosis source to determine criminal responsibility.

propositions.text: Legal concept of 'disease of the mind' excludes self-induced states caused by alcohol or drugs and transitory states (Cooper)
propositions.quote: “disease of the mind” embraces any illness... impairing the human mind... excluding... self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs, as well as transitory mental states

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Cooper defining 'disease of the mind' excluding self-induced intoxication and transitory states.

propositions.text: Court must first consider insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. before considering s. 33.1 Cr. C.; reversing steps is incorrect
propositions.quote: court must not begin its analysis by considering whether the mental condition... is covered by s. 33.1 Cr. C.... The court must instead consider... s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Legal characterization under s. 16 Cr. C. must not depend on causation interpretation under s. 33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: legal characterization exercise required by s. 16 Cr. C. would depend on the interpretation of the concept of causation in issue in s. 33.1 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Court rules analysis must first consider s. 16 insanity defence before s. 33.1 intoxication defence; legal characterization must not depend on s. 33.1 causation.

propositions.text: Whether a toxic psychosis from intoxication is a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C. or excluded by Cooper.
propositions.quote: what remains to be determined is whether a toxic psychosis that results exclusively from a state of intoxication, which the appellant views as an “abnormal effect” of intoxication, constitutes a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. or is excluded by Cooper.

propositions.text: Cooper’s exclusion of self-induced intoxication states applies only to normal effects of intoxication.
propositions.quote: The appellant submits that Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs” applies only to the normal effects of intoxication (transcript, at p. 20).

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue whether toxic psychosis from intoxication is a mental disorder under s.16 or excluded by Cooper; the appellant argues Cooper excludes only normal intoxication effects.

propositions.text: The appellant’s criticism of the Court of Appeal’s position on ss.16 and 33.1 Cr. C. is unfounded.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s criticism of the Court of Appeal’s position on the interplay between ss. 16 and 33.1 Cr. C. is unfounded.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. stated no overlap is possible between ss.16 and 33.1 and that psychosis from drug consumption cannot be a disease of the mind under s.16.
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A. did not infer that s. 33.1 Cr. C. limits the scope of the defence of mental disorder provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. She stated clearly that no overlap is possible in the application of these provisions and simply concluded that, as the law stands in Canada, [translation] “an accused suffering from a psychosis caused by the consumption of drugs in circumstances analogous to the ones in the case before us” cannot be found to have a disease of the mind for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: The appellant was legally intoxicated at the material time and his argument was an indirect way to avoid s.33.1 application.
propositions.quote: After noting that the appellant had to be considered from a legal standpoint to have been intoxicated at the material time, Thibault J.A. added that the appellant’s argument was an indirect way to avoid the application of s. 33.1 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's criticism of the Court of Appeal is unfounded; Thibault J.A. found no overlap between ss.16 and 33.1 and that appellant was legally intoxicated.

propositions.text: Whether the Court of Appeal erred in law by applying s.33.1 Cr. C. instead of s.16 Cr. C. in this case.
propositions.quote: the fundamental issue at this point is whether the Court of Appeal erred in law in holding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. was applicable in this case rather than s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the fundamental issue is whether the Court of Appeal erred in applying s.33.1 instead of s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: The defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder protects the criminal justice system's integrity and fundamental principles.
propositions.quote: a verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder protects the integrity of our country’s criminal justice system and the collective interest in ensuring respect for its fundamental principles.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the defence protects the criminal justice system's integrity and fundamental principles.

propositions.text: Criminal responsibility requires a voluntary act; unfair to punish involuntary acts.
propositions.quote: criminal responsibility can result only from the commission of a voluntary act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states criminal responsibility requires a voluntary act; involuntary acts are unfairly punished.

propositions.text: An act is voluntary if it results from free will; no actus reus without willing mind.
propositions.quote: there can be no actus reus unless it is the result of a willing mind at liberty to make a definite choice or decision

propositions.text: Taschereau J. in R. v. King stated voluntariness requires willpower to do an act regardless of knowledge of illegality.
propositions.quote: there can be no actus reus unless it is the result of a willing mind at liberty to make a definite choice or decision, or in other words, there must be a willpower to do an act whether the accused knew or not that it was prohibited by law

propositions.text: Dickson J.'s dissent in Rabey, endorsed in Parks, held no criminal responsibility for involuntary acts.
propositions.quote: no one can be found criminally responsible for an involuntary act (see Dickson J.’s dissenting reasons in Rabey v. The Queen, which were endorsed on this point in R. v. Parks)

paragraphs.summary: The court explains voluntariness requires free will; cites R. v. King and Rabey for no criminal responsibility for involuntary acts.

propositions.text: Will is expressed by conscious control over body; voluntariness includes physical and moral control.
propositions.quote: An individual’s will is expressed through conscious control exerted by the individual over his or her body

propositions.text: Perka explains voluntariness relates to physical muscle movements and moral control over actions.
propositions.quote: The control may be physical, in which case voluntariness relates to the muscle movements of a person exerting physical control over his or her body. The exercise of a person’s will may also involve moral control over actions the person wants to take

propositions.text: Voluntary act is a carefully thought out act performed freely with minimum intelligence.
propositions.quote: a voluntary act is a carefully thought out act that is performed freely by an individual with at least a minimum level of intelligence

propositions.text: Will is also a product of reason.
propositions.quote: Will is also a product of reason.

paragraphs.summary: The court states will is conscious control over body, including physical and moral control; voluntary acts require reason and intelligence.

propositions.text: Criminal law views individuals as autonomous, rational beings; voluntariness reflects this moral dimension.
propositions.quote: The moral dimension of the voluntary act, which this Court recognized in Perka, thus reflects the idea that the criminal law views individuals as autonomous and rational beings.

propositions.text: Alexander and Ferzan say autonomy and reason are cornerstones of criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: this idea can be seen as the cornerstone of the principles governing the attribution of criminal responsibility

propositions.text: R. v. Ruzic states criminal responsibility requires voluntary act and guilty mind rooted in autonomy and free will.
propositions.quote: The treatment of criminal offenders as rational, autonomous and choosing agents is a fundamental organizing principle of our criminal law... requirement of a guilty mind is rooted in respect for individual autonomy and free will

paragraphs.summary: The court explains criminal law sees individuals as autonomous and rational; voluntariness and guilty mind reflect autonomy and free will.

propositions.text: Presumption that individuals can distinguish right from wrong; rebuttable by proof of incapacity.
propositions.quote: This essential basis for attributing criminal responsibility thus gives rise to a presumption that each individual can distinguish right from wrong.

propositions.text: R. v. Chaulk states criminal responsibility requires discerning moral agent capable of choosing right from wrong.
propositions.quote: there is “a fundamental conviction that criminal responsibility is appropriate only where the actor is a discerning moral agent, capable of making choices between right and wrong”

propositions.text: Ruzic recognizes principle that only voluntary conduct should attract criminal liability.
propositions.quote: only voluntary conduct — behaviour that is the product of a free will and controlled body, unhindered by external constraints — should attract the penalty and stigma of criminal liability

paragraphs.summary: The court states a presumption of moral capacity exists but can be rebutted; only voluntary conduct attracts criminal liability.

propositions.text: Insanity is an exception; a person with mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C. lacks capacity to appreciate nature or wrongness of acts.
propositions.quote: A person suffering from a mental disorder within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. is not considered to be capable of appreciating the nature of his or her acts or understanding that they are inherently wrong.

propositions.text: Lamer C.J. in Chaulk said insanity provisions exempt from criminal liability due to incapacity for intent.
propositions.quote: the insanity provisions of the Criminal Code “operate, at the most fundamental level, as an exemption from criminal liability which is predicated on an incapacity for criminal intent”

paragraphs.summary: The court states insanity under s.16 Cr. C. exempts from criminal liability due to incapacity to appreciate acts or their wrongness.

propositions.text: An insane person is incapable of morally voluntary conduct; their actions are not from free will.
propositions.quote: it can also be said that an insane person is incapable of morally voluntary conduct. The person’s actions are not actually the product of his or her free will.

propositions.text: It is consistent with fundamental justice to exempt persons covered by s.16 Cr. C. from criminal responsibility.
propositions.quote: It is therefore consistent with the principles of fundamental justice for a person whose mental condition at the relevant time is covered by s. 16 Cr. C. not to be criminally responsible under Canadian law.

propositions.text: Convicting involuntary actors undermines criminal law and judicial system integrity.
propositions.quote: Convicting a person who acted involuntarily would undermine the foundations of the criminal law and the integrity of the judicial system.

paragraphs.summary: The court states insane persons lack moral voluntariness; exempting them from criminal responsibility aligns with fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Mental disorder defence leads to not criminally responsible verdict triggering administrative process for public safety and care.
propositions.quote: That verdict triggers an administrative process whose purpose is to determine whether the accused is a significant threat to the safety of the public, to take any necessary action to control that threat and, if necessary, to provide the accused with appropriate care.

propositions.text: Not criminally responsible verdict balances treating morally innocent offenders and protecting public.
propositions.quote: A verdict of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder thus gives effect to society’s interest in ensuring that morally innocent offenders are treated rather than punished, while protecting the public as fully as possible.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the mental disorder defence leads to a not criminally responsible verdict balancing offender treatment and public protection.

propositions.text: Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code governs management of accused found not criminally responsible.
propositions.quote: An accused who is found not criminally responsible becomes subject to the scheme established in Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: R. v. Swain held automatic indeterminate detention of NCR accused violated s.7 Charter right to liberty.
propositions.quote: this Court had held in R. v. Swain, that a Criminal Code provision requiring the automatic and indeterminate detention of an accused found not criminally responsible violated the right to liberty guaranteed by s. 7 of the Charter .

propositions.text: Winko explains Part XX.1 replaces common law regime with individualized assessment and treatment for NCR accused.
propositions.quote: In Winko... explained the principles underlying the application of Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code as follows:... emphasizing individualized assessment and the provision of opportunities for appropriate treatment.

propositions.text: NCR finding is not a finding of dangerousness but triggers assessment of dangerousness and treatment needs.
propositions.quote: This is not a finding of dangerousness. It is rather a finding that triggers a balanced assessment of the offender’s possible dangerousness and of what treatment‑associated measures are required to offset it.

propositions.text: NCR accused must be treated with dignity and maximum liberty compatible with public protection and fairness.
propositions.quote: Throughout the process the offender is to be treated with dignity and accorded the maximum liberty compatible with Part XX.1’s goals of public protection and fairness to the NCR accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Part XX.1 governs NCR accused management, emphasizing individualized assessment, dignity, and balancing liberty with public protection.

propositions.text: Will review s.16 Cr. C. conditions and consider issues related to toxic psychoses from self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: I will now review the conditions that must be met for s. 16 Cr. C. to apply... then consider issues related specifically to toxic psychoses that result from a state of self‑induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court will review s.16 conditions and then consider toxic psychoses from self-induced intoxication.

propositions.text: s.16(2) Cr. C. presumes no mental disorder; accused must prove mental disorder causing incapacity on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: Section 16(2) Cr. C. provides that “[e]very person is presumed not to suffer from a mental disorder so as to be exempt from criminal responsibility”. An accused who seeks to avoid criminal responsibility on this ground must prove on a balance of probabilities that, at the material time, he or she was suffering from “a mental disorder that rendered the person incapable of appreciating the nature and quality of the act or omission or of knowing that it was wrong” (s. 16(1) Cr. C.).

propositions.text: Chaulk held burden on accused infringes presumption of innocence but is a reasonable limit.
propositions.quote: In Chaulk, this Court held that imposing this burden of proof on the accused infringed the presumption of innocence guaranteed by s. 11 (d) of the Charter but that this was nonetheless a reasonable limit

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.16 presumes no mental disorder; accused must prove incapacity; Chaulk held this burden is a reasonable limit on presumption of innocence.

propositions.text: Defence requires two-stage test: characterize mental disorder and determine incapacity to know act was wrong.
propositions.quote: An accused who wishes to successfully raise the defence of mental disorder must therefore meet the requirements of a two‑stage statutory test... characterize the mental state... and determine incapacity to know that the act was wrong.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the defence requires a two-stage test: mental disorder characterization and incapacity to know wrongness.

propositions.text: It is undisputed appellant was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at material time.
propositions.quote: it is not in dispute that the appellant was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at the material time.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant was in serious psychotic condition and unaware of his acts at the time.
propositions.quote: [a]t the time the criminal acts were committed, the accused did not realize what he was doing and was in a serious psychotic condition; there is no real dispute about this

propositions.text: Only issue is whether psychosis resulted from a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: the only issue in this appeal is whether the psychosis resulted from a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellant's incapacity to distinguish right from wrong is undisputed; issue is whether psychosis is a mental disorder under s.16.

propositions.text: Criminal Code defines 'mental disorder' as 'disease of the mind' but is circular and courts must delineate it.
propositions.quote: The Criminal Code does not contain a precise definition of the “mental disorder” concept for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. Section 2 Cr. C. simply provides that the term “mental disorder” means “a disease of the mind”

paragraphs.summary: The court states Criminal Code defines 'mental disorder' as 'disease of the mind' but courts must delineate it.

propositions.text: Cooper defines 'disease of the mind' broadly as any illness impairing mind and its functioning.
propositions.quote: the “disease of the mind” concept includes “any illness, disorder or abnormal condition which impairs the human mind and its functioning”

propositions.text: Rabey states concept embraces mental disorders of organic and functional origin, curable or not, temporary or not.
propositions.quote: the concept is broad, embracing mental disorders of organic and functional origin, whether curable or incurable, temporary or not, recurring or non‑recurring

propositions.text: Definition is inclusive to protect public from persons who could be threats.
propositions.quote: the inclusive nature of the definition of “mental disorder” can be explained in particular by Parliament’s wish to give the public a high level of protection from persons who could be a threat to others

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Cooper and Rabey defining 'disease of the mind' broadly to include many disorders, reflecting Parliament's public protection intent.

propositions.text: Mental disorder concept evolves with medical science and cannot be precisely defined.
propositions.quote: The “mental disorder” concept continues to evolve, which means that it can be adapted continually to advances in medical science... this concept “is not capable of precise definition”

propositions.text: Concept is flexible to apply to any mental condition impairing mind and compatible with s.16 policy.
propositions.quote: It is thus flexible enough to apply to any mental condition that... is indicative of a disorder that impairs the human mind or its functioning, and the recognition of which is compatible with the policy considerations that underlie the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the mental disorder concept evolves with medical science and is flexible to apply to impairing conditions compatible with s.16 policy.

propositions.text: Disease of the mind is a legal concept with a medical dimension decided by the trial judge, not the jury.
propositions.quote: For the purposes of the Criminal Code , “disease of the mind” is a legal concept with a medical dimension. Although medical expertise plays an essential part in the legal characterization exercise, it has long been established in positive law that whether a particular mental condition can be characterized as a “mental disorder” is a question of law to be decided by the trial judge. In a jury trial, the judge decides this question, not the jury.

propositions.text: Psychiatrists describe mental condition medically; judge decides if it fits 'disease of the mind'.
propositions.quote: As Martin J.A. stated in an oft‑quoted passage from Simpson, “[i]t is the function of the psychiatrist to describe the accused’s mental condition and how it is considered from the medical point of view. It is for the Judge to decide whether the condition described is comprehended by the term ‘disease of the mind’” (p. 350).

propositions.text: If judge finds mental condition is a mental disorder, jury decides if accused had it at offence time.
propositions.quote: If the judge finds as a matter of law that the mental condition of the accused is a “mental disorder”, it will ultimately be up to the jury to decide whether, on the facts, the accused was suffering from such a mental disorder at the time of the offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that 'disease of the mind' is a legal question for the judge, with medical experts describing condition; jury decides factual presence at offence time.

propositions.text: Trial judge is not bound by medical evidence as experts ignore policy aspects of s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: Thus, the trial judge is not bound by the medical evidence, since medical experts generally take no account of the policy component of the analysis required by s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Expert opinion on legal issue of mental disorder has little evidentiary value.
propositions.quote: Moreover, an expert’s opinion on the legal issue of whether the mental condition of the accused constitutes a “mental disorder” within the meaning of the Criminal Code has “little or no evidentiary value” (R. v. Luedecke, 2008 ONCA 716, 269 O.A.C. 1, at para. 113).

paragraphs.summary: The court states trial judges are not bound by medical evidence and expert opinions on legal mental disorder issues have little evidentiary value.

propositions.text: Stone summarized roles: legal question, mixed law and fact, and factual question for trier of fact.
propositions.quote: The respective roles of the expert, the judge and the jury were summarized in R. v. Stone, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 290. Writing for the majority, Bastarache J. stated the following: Taken alone, the question of what mental conditions are included in the term “disease of the mind” is a question of law. However, the trial judge must also determine whether the condition the accused claims to have suffered from satisfies the legal test for disease of the mind. This involves an assessment of the particular evidence in the case rather than a general principle of law and is thus a question of mixed law and fact. . . . The question of whether the accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind is a question of fact to be determined by the trier of fact. [Citation omitted; para. 197.]

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Stone explaining the legal, mixed, and factual roles of judge, expert, and jury in disease of the mind analysis.

propositions.text: Central issue: whether toxic psychosis from single intoxication episode is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: The central issue in this appeal is a question of law within the meaning of Stone. It is common ground that the appellant was in a psychotic condition that prevented him from distinguishing right from wrong. The main issue is whether a toxic psychosis caused exclusively by a single episode of intoxication constitutes a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the central legal issue as whether toxic psychosis from a single intoxication episode is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr.C.

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis must always be a mental disorder, making diagnosis determinative.
propositions.quote: To argue that toxic psychosis must always be considered a “mental disorder” is to say that the legal characterization exercise under s. 16 Cr. C. depends exclusively on a medical diagnosis.

propositions.text: This argument conflicts with case law and improperly shifts responsibility from judge/jury to expert.
propositions.quote: If the appellant’s position were accepted, psychiatric experts would thus be responsible for determining the scope of the defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder. This argument conflicts directly with this Court’s consistent case law over the past three decades and cannot succeed. It would shift the responsibility for deciding whether the accused is guilty from the judge or jury to the expert.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the appellant's argument that toxic psychosis is always a mental disorder, as it conflicts with case law and improperly shifts decision-making to experts.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is medically diagnosed but its causes vary widely and are not always precisely identified.
propositions.quote: An additional reason for rejecting the appellant’s central argument has to do with the very diverse reality encompassed by the term “toxic psychosis”. In the case law, this term usually refers to the symptoms of the accused as diagnosed by psychiatrists. However, medical science does not always identify the causes of toxic psychosis as precisely as is required in law.

propositions.text: Case law shows toxic psychosis arises in diverse circumstances related to toxic substance exposure.
propositions.quote: Although toxic psychosis is always related to exposure to a toxic substance, the circumstances in which it may arise can vary a great deal. This is readily apparent from a review of the case law on this point (see R. v. Oakley (1986), 24 C.C.C. (3d) 351 (Ont. C.A.); R. v. Mailloux (1985), 25 C.C.C. (3d) 171 (Ont. C.A.), aff’d [1988] 2 S.C.R. 1029; R. v. Moroz, 2003 ABPC 5, 333 A.R. 109; R. v. Snelgrove, 2004 BCSC 102 (CanLII); R. v. Lauv, 2004 BCSC 1093 (CanLII); R. v. Fortin, 2005 CanLII 6933 (C.Q.); R. v. Paul, 2011 BCCA 46, 299 B.C.A.C. 85).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes toxic psychosis is medically diagnosed but its causes vary widely, as shown by case law.

propositions.text: Many factors contribute to substance-induced psychosis, varying by individual and drug use.
propositions.quote: Many factors might contribute to a state of substance‑induced psychosis, including the fact that symptoms of a paranoid personality disorder are active at the time drugs are taken (Mailloux), the combined effect of exposure to toxic vapours and a period of intense stress (Oakley), dependence on certain drugs, such as cocaine (Moroz and Snelgrove), heavy drug use during the days and hours leading up to the commission of the crime (Lauv and Paul), and withdrawal following a period of excessive drinking (R. v. Malcolm (1989), 50 C.C.C. (3d) 172 (Man. C.A.)). It seems that this diversity of circumstances can be attributed to variations in psychological makeup and psychological histories from one accused to another, as well as in the nature of the drug use that contributed to their psychoses. The quantity and toxicity of the drugs taken also seem to have a significant effect in this regard. As a result, in each new situation, the case turns on its own facts and cannot always be fitted easily into the existing case law.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that substance-induced psychosis arises from many factors varying by individual and drug use, making cases fact-specific.

propositions.text: Rejects appellant's broad approach; endorses cautious, contextual approach from Cooper balancing public safety and responsibility.
propositions.quote: Because of the heterogeneous nature of the circumstances in which a toxic psychosis at the material time may be medically diagnosed, I consider it unwise to adopt an approach as broad as the one proposed by the appellant. In Cooper, this Court instead urged the courts to exercise particular caution where an accused person’s mental condition was closely related to an episode of intoxication contemporaneous with the offence. In my opinion, the Court, in its decision in Cooper, recommended a contextual approach that was intended to strike a fair balance between the need to protect the public from persons whose mental state is inherently dangerous and the desire to impose criminal liability solely on persons who are responsible for the state they were in at the time of the offence.

propositions.text: Contextual approach requires case-specific analysis; toxic psychosis is not always a disease of the mind legally.
propositions.quote: Since this contextual approach means that a court must base its analysis on the particular circumstances of the case before it, I cannot accept the recent decisions or opinions that seem to suggest that toxic psychosis is always a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code (see, inter alia, Snelgrove, at para. 234; Lauv, at para. 18; Fortin, at para. 57; R. v. D.P., 2009 QCCQ 644 (CanLII), at para. 25; and H. Parent, “Les Troubles psychotiques induits par une substance en droit pénal canadien: analyse médicale et juridique d’un concept en pleine évolution” (2010), 69 R. du B. 103, at p. 119).

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the appellant's broad approach, endorsing a cautious, contextual approach from Cooper and rejecting that toxic psychosis is always a disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Court should start from presumption that temporary psychosis from intoxication is excluded under Cooper.
propositions.quote: When confronted with a difficult fact situation involving a state of toxic psychosis that emerged while the accused was intoxicated, a court should start from the general principle that temporary psychosis is covered by the exclusion from Cooper.

propositions.text: Accused can rebut presumption by showing disease of mind unrelated to intoxication symptoms.
propositions.quote: The principle is not absolute, however: the accused can rebut the presumption provided for in s. 16(2) Cr. C. by showing that, at the material time, he or she was suffering from a disease of the mind that was unrelated to the intoxication‑related symptoms.

propositions.text: Court should adopt Stone's 'more holistic approach' to determine if accused's condition is a mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: To determine whether an accused has discharged the burden of proof in this respect, the court should adopt the “more holistic approach” described by Bastarache J. in Stone (para. 203).

propositions.text: Attorney General of Ontario supports holistic approach to determine mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: As the Attorney General of Ontario suggested in this Court, it is ultimately this “more holistic approach” that will enable a court to determine whether the mental condition of an accused at the material time constitutes a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. (Factum, at paras. 22‑23).

paragraphs.summary: The court states courts should presume temporary psychosis from intoxication is excluded, but accused can rebut using Stone's holistic approach, supported by Ontario AG.

propositions.text: Stone proposes flexible approach with two analytical tools and policy considerations to distinguish mental disorders from intoxication states.
propositions.quote: In Stone, Bastarache J. proposed a flexible approach structured around two analytical tools and certain policy considerations. The purpose of the approach is to help the courts distinguish mental conditions that fall within the scope of s. 16 Cr. C. from those covered by Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs” (p. 1159).

propositions.text: Approach helps determine if medically diagnosed disease of mind is a legal mental disorder.
propositions.quote: In other words, a court should use this approach to determine whether a medically diagnosed disease of the mind constitutes a mental disorder in the legal sense.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone's flexible approach with two analytical tools to distinguish legal mental disorders from intoxication states.

propositions.text: First analytical tool: internal cause factor compares accused to normal person to assess trigger nature.
propositions.quote: The internal cause factor, the first of the analytical tools described in Stone, involves comparing the accused with a normal person. In that case, Bastarache J. noted that “the trial judge must consider the nature of the trigger and determine whether a normal person in the same circumstances might have reacted to it by entering an automatistic state as the accused claims to have done” (para. 206).

propositions.text: If normal person might react similarly, trigger is external and excludes condition from s.16 Cr.C. mental disorder scope.
propositions.quote: The comparison between the circumstances of the accused and those of a normal person will be objective and may be based on the psychiatric evidence. The more the psychiatric evidence suggests that a normal person, that is, a person suffering from no disease of the mind, is susceptible to such a state, the more justified the courts will be in finding that the trigger is external. Such a finding would exclude the condition of the accused from the scope of s. 16 Cr. C. The reverse also holds true.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone's first analytical tool: comparing accused to normal person to determine if trigger is external, excluding mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.

propositions.text: Trigger can be alcohol or drugs; court must consider all consumption circumstances for normal person's likely reaction.
propositions.quote: Although the trigger associated with the internal cause factor often involves a “psychological blow”, there is no reason why it cannot consist of alcohol or drug use contemporaneous with the offence. What must therefore be determined is what state a normal person might have entered after consuming the same substances in the same quantities as the accused. Since certain factors such as fatigue and the pace of consumption may influence the effects of drugs, this comparison must take account of all the circumstances in which the accused consumed the drugs that triggered the psychotic condition.

propositions.text: If normal person might develop toxic psychosis from similar drug use, mental disorder is external and excluded from s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: If a normal person might also have reacted to similar drug use by developing toxic psychosis, it will be easier for the court to find that the mental disorder of the accused was purely external in origin (Rabey (S.C.C.), at pp. 519 and 533; see also Moroz, at para. 46) and was not a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The court states trigger can be drugs; courts must consider all circumstances to see if normal person might develop toxic psychosis, excluding mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.

propositions.text: Second analytical tool: continuing danger factor assesses likelihood of recurring danger to others.
propositions.quote: The second analytical tool, the continuing danger factor, is directly related to the need to ensure public safety. The purpose of this factor is to assess the likelihood of recurring danger to others.

propositions.text: Greater likelihood of recurring danger increases chance condition is a disease of the mind.
propositions.quote: Where a condition is likely to present a recurring danger, there is a greater chance that it will be regarded as a disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Court must consider psychiatric history and likelihood trigger will recur to assess danger.
propositions.quote: To assess this danger, the court must consider, among other factors, “the psychiatric history of the accused and the likelihood that the trigger alleged to have caused the automatistic episode will recur” (Stone, at para. 214).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone's second analytical tool: continuing danger factor assessing recurring danger likelihood, considering psychiatric history and trigger recurrence.

propositions.text: Recurring danger must arise independently of accused's will to be relevant to disease of mind.
propositions.quote: Although Bastarache J.’s reasons were not explicit in this regard, it stands to reason that danger will be recurring only if it is likely to arise again independently of the exercise of the will of the accused.

propositions.text: Danger from voluntary future drug use is not a mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: The recurrence of danger is not a factor linked to voluntary behaviour by the accused. This conclusion is consistent with the idea that the effect of the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. is to exempt from criminal responsibility an accused whose actions are morally involuntary. The purpose of the defence of mental disorder is to ascertain whether the mental condition of the accused poses an inherent danger, that is, a danger that persists despite the will of the accused. As a corollary to this principle, a danger to public safety that might be voluntarily created by the accused in the future by consuming drugs would not be the result of a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states recurring danger must be independent of accused's will; danger from voluntary drug use is not a mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.

propositions.text: Holistic approach allows consideration of policy concerns, mainly protecting society via Part XX.1 Cr.C.
propositions.quote: In Stone, Bastarache J. also stated that “a holistic approach to disease of the mind must also permit trial judges to consider other policy concerns which underlie this inquiry” (para. 218). The main policy consideration continues to be the need to protect society from the accused through the special procedure set out in Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: If pre-existing condition needs no treatment and is not a threat, court should more easily find no disease of the mind.
propositions.quote: Thus, if the circumstances of a case suggest that a pre‑existing condition of the accused does not require any particular treatment and is not a threat to others, the court should more easily hold that the accused was not suffering from a disease of the mind at the time of the alleged events.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone's holistic approach includes policy concerns, mainly public protection, and courts should more easily find no disease of mind if no treatment or threat needed.

propositions.text: Contextual approach defines appeal scope; no exhaustive rule for all toxic psychosis cases.
propositions.quote: The contextual approach required by Stone makes it possible to define the scope of this appeal. The purpose of the appeal is not to identify a rule to be applied to every case of toxic psychosis.

propositions.text: Each case has distinctive characteristics; exhaustive definition of Cooper's exclusion is counterproductive.
propositions.quote: And because every case has distinctive characteristics, it would be counterproductive to try to formulate an exhaustive definition of the mental conditions covered by Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs”.

propositions.text: This case concerns toxic psychosis from a single episode of self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: The instant case concerns just one type of toxic psychosis, namely one that resulted exclusively from a single episode of self‑induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the contextual approach limits appeal scope; no exhaustive rule for toxic psychosis; this case involves single episode self-induced intoxication.

propositions.text: Courts should do individualized analysis applying Stone's holistic approach to each toxic psychosis case.
propositions.quote: Although the courts can seek assistance from the existing case law, it would be preferable for them to engage in an individualized analysis that takes account of the specific circumstances of each case. This means that the courts should determine on a case‑by‑case basis, applying the “more holistic approach” from Stone, whether the mental condition of each accused is included in or excluded from the definition of “disease of the mind” proposed by Dickson J. in Cooper.

propositions.text: This approach aligns with Rabey endorsing case-by-case decisions for transient mental disturbances.
propositions.quote: This approach is consistent with the line of authority based on Rabey, in which this Court endorsed Martin J.A.’s opinion that “[p]articular transient mental disturbances may not . . . be capable of being properly categorized in relation to whether they constitute ‘disease of the mind’ on the basis of a generalized statement and must be decided on a case‑by‑case basis” (pp. 519‑20).

paragraphs.summary: The court says courts should apply Stone's holistic approach case-by-case, consistent with Rabey's endorsement of individualized decisions for transient disturbances.

propositions.text: Court will determine if appellant had mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C. using trial judge's findings.
propositions.quote: In accordance with the approach set out above, I must now determine whether the appellant was suffering from a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. at the material time. To do this, it will be helpful to begin by referring to the trial judge’s main findings of fact.

propositions.text: Trial judge found appellant highly intoxicated and in psychotic condition caused by voluntary drug use.
propositions.quote: Judge Decoste found that the appellant, who was highly intoxicated at the material time, was in a psychotic condition caused by the voluntary consumption of drugs.

propositions.text: Psychotic condition originated in drug use moments before criminal acts.
propositions.quote: He wrote that [translation] “the psychotic condition the accused was in when he committed these criminal acts originated in his drug use during the moments leading up to them” (para. 41).

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis is necessarily a mental disorder as an abnormal intoxication effect affecting predisposed or fragile psyches.
propositions.quote: I would also note that the appellant’s central argument is based on the contention that toxic psychosis is necessarily a “mental disorder” within the meaning of s. 16 Cr. C. because it is an “abnormal effect” of intoxication that affects only those who have a psychological predisposition or whose psyches are particularly fragile.

paragraphs.summary: The court will decide if appellant had a mental disorder using trial judge's findings that appellant was intoxicated and psychotic from voluntary drug use; appellant argues toxic psychosis is necessarily a mental disorder.

propositions.text: Evidence does not support appellant's distinction between normal and abnormal intoxication effects or predisposition argument.
propositions.quote: The evidence in the record does not support the distinction drawn by the appellant between “normal effects” and “abnormal effects” of intoxication. Nor is it compatible with the argument that only persons who are predisposed to a mental disorder are likely to develop toxic psychosis as a result of drug use.

propositions.text: Dr. Faucher testified he sees toxic psychosis cases weekly; 50% of PCP users likely develop psychosis when intoxicated.
propositions.quote: For example, Dr. Faucher testified at trial that he saw cases of toxic psychosis [translation] “every week” (A.R., at p. 967). As Thibault J.A. noted, the same witness also stated that half (50 percent) of subjects who take drugs containing PCP are likely to develop a psychotic condition when intoxicated.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is a fairly frequent phenomenon resulting from high toxicity of chemical drugs.
propositions.quote: It thus appears that toxic psychosis is unfortunately a fairly frequent phenomenon that seems to result from the high toxicity of chemical drugs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence does not support appellant's distinction or predisposition argument; toxic psychosis is frequent and linked to drug toxicity.

propositions.text: Stone's first factor suggests normal person would develop toxic psychosis from one 'poire bleue' pill, contradicting appellant.
propositions.quote: The application of the first factor from Stone thus suggests that the taking of one “poire bleue” pill is a specific external factor that contradicts the appellant’s argument, since it seems likely that the reaction of a normal person to such a pill would indeed be to develop toxic psychosis.

propositions.text: This suggests appellant was not suffering from a mental disorder at the time of the acts.
propositions.quote: This strongly suggests that the appellant was not suffering from a mental disorder at the time he committed the impugned acts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Stone's first factor suggests a normal person would develop toxic psychosis from the pill, indicating appellant lacked a mental disorder then.

propositions.text: Rapid psychotic symptoms indicate delusions are due to an external factor, here toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: The rapid appearance of psychotic symptoms generally indicates that the delusions of the accused can be attributed to a specific external factor.
