propositions.text: Dr. Faucher's expert assessment preferred, showing rapid symptom reversal characteristic of toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: Dr. Faucher’s expert assessment, which the trial judge preferred to that of Dr. Turmel, an expert called by the defence, revealed that the rapid reversal of symptoms is characteristic of a toxic psychosis caused by an episode of self‑induced intoxication

propositions.text: Delusions subsiding with drug effects usually indicate substance intoxication, not a disease of the mind under the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: delusions that subside at the same rate as the drug are usually signs of Substance Intoxication

propositions.text: Such delusions do not result from a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: Such delusions therefore do not result from a disease of the mind within the meaning of the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds rapid psychotic symptoms indicate toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication, not a disease of the mind under the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Appellant's psychotic symptoms diminished after taking 'poire bleue' pill and disappeared by October 28, 2005.
propositions.quote: the psychotic symptoms experienced by the appellant began to diminish shortly after he took the “poire bleue” pill and continued to do so until they disappeared completely on October 28, 2005.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held symptoms disappearance showed toxic psychosis coincided with appellant's intoxication duration.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal held that the disappearance of the symptoms showed that the symptoms of toxic psychosis coincided with the duration of the appellant’s intoxication.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. said appellant had no disease of the mind before crimes and was sane after drug effects passed.
propositions.quote: Thibault J.A. could thus say that “[t]he appellant suffered from no [disease of the mind] before committing the crimes, and once the effects of the drug consumption had passed, he was entirely sane”

propositions.text: Court sees no valid reason to depart from Court of Appeal's conclusion.
propositions.quote: I see no valid reason to depart from this conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the Court of Appeal that appellant's symptoms matched intoxication duration and he was sane after drug effects ended.

propositions.text: No evidence shows appellant's mental condition is inherently dangerous.
propositions.quote: there is no evidence indicating that the mental condition of the accused is inherently dangerous in any way.

propositions.text: If appellant abstains voluntarily from drugs, his mental condition poses no public safety threat.
propositions.quote: Provided that the appellant abstains from such drugs in the future, which he is capable of doing voluntarily, it would seem that his mental condition poses no threat to public safety.

propositions.text: If appellant had drug dependency affecting voluntary abstinence, risk of recurring danger might be greater.
propositions.quote: I might have concluded otherwise if the appellant had a dependency on drugs that affected his ability to stop using them voluntarily. The likelihood of recurring danger might then be greater.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence appellant's mental condition is dangerous if he abstains voluntarily from drugs, but dependency might increase risk.

propositions.text: No valid reason to initiate special procedure under Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code in this case.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that there is no valid reason to initiate the special procedure provided for in Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Accused with mental condition solely from temporary self-induced intoxication and no threat to others is not suffering from 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: An accused whose mental condition at the material time can be attributed exclusively to a state of temporary self‑induced intoxication and who poses no threat to others is not suffering from a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Part XX.1 applies only if accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind at the material time, not to temporary intoxication-induced madness.
propositions.quote: The scheme of Part XX.1 applies only if the accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind at the material time. It is not intended to apply to accused persons whose temporary madness was induced artificially by a state of intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Part XX.1 does not apply as appellant's mental condition was from temporary self-induced intoxication, not a disease of the mind.

propositions.text: Appellant was not suffering from a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. at assault time.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the appellant was not suffering from a “mental disorder” for the purposes of s. 16 Cr. C. at the time he committed the assault.

propositions.text: Appellant failed to rebut presumption that toxic psychosis was self-induced by alcohol or drugs per Cooper definition.
propositions.quote: He has failed to rebut the presumption that his toxic psychosis was a “self‑induced stat[e] caused by alcohol or drugs” in accordance with the definition in Cooper.

propositions.text: Malfunctioning mind from self-induced intoxication is not a disease of the mind legally, even if medical science says otherwise.
propositions.quote: A malfunctioning of the mind that results exclusively from self‑induced intoxication cannot be considered a disease of the mind in the legal sense, since it is not a product of the individual’s inherent psychological makeup.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is a symptom of self-induced intoxication, not a basis to exempt from criminal responsibility under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: toxic psychosis seems to be nothing more than a symptom, albeit an extreme one, of the accused person’s state of self‑induced intoxication. Such a state cannot justify exempting an accused from criminal responsibility under s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's toxic psychosis was self-induced intoxication, not a mental disorder, so no exemption from criminal responsibility under s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Conclusion aligns with policy considerations from Cooper by Dickson J.
propositions.quote: This conclusion takes account of the policy considerations referred to by Dickson J. in Cooper.

propositions.text: Dr. Faucher's expert assessment shows toxic psychosis frequency in similar cases.
propositions.quote: In light of Dr. Faucher’s expert assessment of the frequency of toxic psychosis in circumstances analogous to the ones in the instant case

propositions.text: Appellant's position would broaden s.16 Cr. C. defence scope beyond Parliament's intent, affecting criminal justice integrity.
propositions.quote: the appellant’s position, if adopted, would affect the integrity of the criminal justice system in ways that would be difficult to accept.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis is covered by Cooper's exclusion of self-induced states caused by alcohol or drugs.
propositions.quote: These considerations reinforce the conclusion that the toxic psychosis of the appellant in this case is covered by Cooper’s exclusion of “self‑induced states caused by alcohol or drugs”.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds that policy and expert evidence support excluding toxic psychosis from s.16 defence, preserving criminal justice integrity.

propositions.text: No evidence appellant had underlying mental disorder simplifies legal characterization under s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: The lack of evidence that the appellant was suffering from an underlying mental disorder certainly simplifies the legal characterization exercise under s. 16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Case facts are clear: appellant's mental condition fits Cooper's exclusion for self-induced intoxication.
propositions.quote: From a factual standpoint, this case seems quite clear: as in Paul, the only reasonable conclusion is that the appellant’s mental condition is covered by the exclusion from Cooper.

propositions.text: Appellant asks court to assume toxic psychosis caused by underlying mental disorder without evidence.
propositions.quote: Contrary to the conclusion the appellant is asking this Court to draw, it would be unreasonable to assume, absent any evidence to back up such a claim, that the real cause of his toxic psychosis was an underlying mental disorder.

propositions.text: No Canadian court applied s.16 defence for toxic psychosis without evidence of underlying disease of the mind.
propositions.quote: no Canadian court has applied the defence provided for in s. 16 Cr. C. in the context of toxic psychosis without evidence showing that the accused suffered from an underlying disease of the mind.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of underlying mental disorder and rejects appellant's claim that toxic psychosis was caused by one.

propositions.text: Courts will face harder cases where mental disorder and toxic psychosis coexist triggered by drug use.
propositions.quote: it is plausible to expect that the courts will have to perform this legal characterization exercise in circumstances much more difficult than the ones in the case at bar.

propositions.text: Courts should apply Stone's 'more holistic approach' carefully in complex cases with underlying disorder and drug-triggered psychosis.
propositions.quote: In such circumstances, the courts should be especially meticulous in applying the “more holistic approach” from Stone.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes future cases with underlying disorder and drug-triggered psychosis require careful application of Stone's holistic approach.

propositions.text: Question arises whether s.33.1 Cr. C. applies given appellant's intoxication and conduct.
propositions.quote: The foregoing conclusion leads to the question whether s. 33.1 Cr. C. is applicable.

propositions.text: s.33.1 Cr. C. applies if accused was intoxicated, self-induced intoxication, and departed from reasonable care by threatening bodily integrity.
propositions.quote: This provision applies where three conditions are met: (1) the accused was intoxicated at the material time; (2) the intoxication was self‑induced; and (3) the accused departed from the standard of reasonable care generally recognized in Canadian society by interfering or threatening to interfere with the bodily integrity of another person

propositions.text: If these conditions met, lack of general intent or voluntariness is not a defence under s.33.1 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: Where these three things are proved, it is not a defence that the accused lacked the general intent or the voluntariness required to commit the offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises whether s.33.1 applies, which removes defence if accused self-induced intoxication and threatened bodily integrity.

propositions.text: Self-induced intoxication under s.33.1 Cr. C. is limited to period substance produces effects.
propositions.quote: The self‑induced intoxication to which s. 33.1 Cr. C. refers is limited in time. It corresponds to the period during which the substance consumed by the accused produced its effects.

propositions.text: s.33.1(2) Cr. C. states person is criminally at fault if in self-induced intoxication state and interferes with bodily integrity.
propositions.quote: Section 33.1(2) Cr. C. leaves no doubt about this. It provides that a person “is . . . criminally at fault where the person, while in a state of self‑induced intoxication that renders the person unaware of, or incapable of consciously controlling, their behaviour, voluntarily or involuntarily interferes or threatens to interfere with the bodily integrity of another person”.

propositions.text: s.33.1 Cr. C. prevents accused avoiding liability by claiming intoxication negated mental element or voluntariness.
propositions.quote: Section 33.1 Cr. C. is intended to prevent an accused from avoiding criminal liability on the ground that his or her state of intoxication at the material time rendered the accused incapable of forming the mental element or having the voluntariness required to commit the offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.33.1 applies during intoxication effects and prevents intoxication negating criminal liability.

propositions.text: s.33.1 Cr. C. applies to any mental condition directly from intoxication, including toxic psychosis.
propositions.quote: Section 33.1 Cr. C. therefore applies to any mental condition that is a direct extension of a state of intoxication.

propositions.text: Appellant wrongly suggests s.33.1 applies only to 'normal effects' of intoxication.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s suggestion that it applies only to the “normal effects” of intoxication is wrong.

propositions.text: No intoxication threshold excludes s.33.1 application; toxic psychosis is covered and applies here.
propositions.quote: There is no threshold of intoxication beyond which s. 33.1 Cr. C. does not apply to an accused, which means that toxic psychosis can be one of the states of intoxication covered by this provision. It is so covered in the case at bar.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal correctly held s.33.1 Cr. C. applicable rather than s.16 Cr. C.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal therefore did not err in law in holding that s. 33.1 Cr. C. was applicable rather than s. 16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellant's claim and holds s.33.1 applies to toxic psychosis; Court of Appeal was correct.

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, the appeal must be dismissed. Appeal dismissed.
